name: Agastya (Akattiyar)
summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition, Akattiyar (Kuṟumuṉi, Kumpamuṉi) is the first and foremost of the Siddhars and the founder of Siddha medicine: sent south by Śiva to the Potiyil hills, he received Tamil from Śiva or Murukaṉ, composed the lost grammar Akattiyam, and is the author-authority of a large medical, alchemical and yogic corpus and of the vital-point (varmam) lore.
places: Potiyil (Potikai) hills
Kuṟṟālam
Anantaśayanam (Thiruvananthapuram) — samādhi in the popular list

realization_account.text: When all gods and sages gathered in the north for Śiva's wedding and the earth tilted, Śiva sent the diminutive Agastya south, where he balanced the world from the Potiyil hills; he is held to live there still as a Siddhar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: U22 contribution (Tamil Siddha / Siddha medicine). Scholars do not assume the Vedic, epic and Tamil Agastyas are one person, and regard the Tamil medical works under his name as late. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Tirumūlar
summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Tirumūlar heads many lists of the eighteen Siddhars; his Tirumantiram is their root text for eightfold yoga, the eight great powers and the perfecting of the body ('I nourished the body and so nourished the life', TM 724). Later Siddhar works (Tirumūla nāyaṉār ñāṉam, medical treatises) circulate under his name.
places: Chidambaram — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the full entry. TM 69 names his seven (or eight) disciples, among them Kālāṅki and Kañcamalaiyaṉ. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Bogar (Pōkar)
summary: Siddhar of Palani, alchemist and physician: the tradition says he made the image of Murukaṉ as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi at Palani from nine poisonous minerals (navapāṣāṇam), travelled to China (Cīṉam) and flew through the air, and recorded medicine, alchemy and kāya kaṟpam in the 'Seven Thousand' (Pōkar ēḻāyiram). Disciple of Kālāṅki Nātar; teacher of Pulippāṇi, Koṅkaṇar and Karuvūrār.
places: Palani — samādhi within the hill temple (tradition)
China (Cīṉam), in his own account

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

realization_account.text: Bogar is said to have consecrated the navapāṣāṇa image at Palani and to have entered samādhi beneath the shrine, where he abides; his own verses describe journeys to China and flights by the power of kaḷikai pills (recorded as his claim).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Chinese connection is the text's and tradition's claim; modern theories identifying him with a Chinese Taoist are outside the tradition and not recorded. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Sivavākkiyar (Civavākkiyar)
summary: The most iconoclastic Siddhar poet: his Civavākkiyam mocks stone images, temple ritual, pilgrimage, Vedic recitation and caste, locates the Lord within, and in one famous verse denies the rebirth of the dead. His name is explained as 'he whose (first) utterance was Śiva'.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition identifies him with Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār in his Śaiva phase; others reject the identification. Not in the popular list of eighteen, but in other lists and in every Siddhar anthology.

name: Pāmbāṭṭi (Pāmpāṭṭic cittar)
summary: The 'snake-charmer Siddhar', whose songs with the refrain 'dance, O snake!' teach the inner ascent and scorn caste, learning and ritual. The tradition says he was a snake-catcher seeking a jewelled serpent in the hills when a Siddhar (usually Caṭṭaimuṉi) showed him that the true serpent lies coiled within.
places: Marudamalai
Caṅkaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The meeting with Caṭṭaimuṉi is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Iṭaikkāṭar
summary: Shepherd-Siddhar (iṭaiyar) whose songs address the herdsman, cattle and flute. The tradition tells that, foreseeing a twelve-year drought, he fed his flock on erukku leaves and stored grain in mud, and when the nine planets came to him he so charmed them that they shifted their places and the rains returned.
places: Tiruvaṇṇāmalai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Distinct from the Caṅkam poet Iṭaikkāṭaṉār. The planets legend and his discipleship to Bogar are recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Karuvūrār
summary: Siddhar of Karūr; in the tradition a disciple of Bogar who helped Rājarāja Cōḻa set the great liṅga of the Tañcāvūr temple, where he has a shrine; identified with the Tiruvicaippā poet Karuvūrttēvar.
places: Tañcāvūr (shrine in the Bṛhadīśvara temple)
Karūr — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: U22 contribution. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Koṅkaṇar
summary: Siddhar and alchemist, in the tradition a disciple of Bogar. A popular story tells that he burnt a crane with his glance and was then rebuked by a devoted housewife who had kept him waiting: 'Did you take me for the crane, Koṅkaṇa?' — sending him to learn from her and from Tiruvaḷḷuvar.
places: Tirupati — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The crane story (kokkeṉṟu niṉaittāyō koṅkaṇavā) is recalled with moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Caṭṭaimuṉi (Sattaimuni)
summary: Siddhar whose name is taken from the cloak (caṭṭai) he wore; his Ñāṉam contrasts outward worship with the Siddhars' worship of the goddess on the 'Meru' of triangles and with vāci yoga. Some accounts say he wrote openly what other Siddhars veiled.
places: Srirangam — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Origins and the 'open writing' story recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Nandi (Nantīcar)
summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Nandi (Nantīcar, Nantitēvar) is the first of the eighteen Siddhars and the channel through whom Śiva's knowledge — including medicine — reached Tirumūlar and the others (TM 67–68).
places: Kāśī — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Patañjali (as a Tamil Siddhar)
summary: The Tamil tradition counts Patañjali among the eighteen Siddhars and, with Vyāghrapāda, among Nandi's disciples who worshipped at the hall (maṉṟu) of Chidambaram (TM 67); it identifies him with the author of the Yoga Sūtras.
places: Chidambaram
Rāmēśvaram — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution. The identification of the Chidambaram sage, the grammarian and the Yoga Sūtra author is the tradition's; scholars keep them apart. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Vyāghrapāda (Viyākkiramar, Puliyūr muṉi)
summary: The 'tiger-footed' sage who with Patañjali worshipped the Dance at Chidambaram (Puliyūr); named in TM 67 among Nandi's eight disciples.
places: Chidambaram (Puliyūr)

name: Vālmīki (as a Tamil Siddhar)
summary: Counted among the eighteen Siddhars in the popular Tamil list, with a samādhi place at Eṭṭukkuṭi.
places: Eṭṭukkuṭi — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; whether the list intends the epic poet or a Tamil namesake is not settled. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Dhanvantari (Taṉvantiri)
summary: The physician of the gods, counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars in the popular list, with a samādhi place at Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil, the shrine of Śiva as the divine physician.
places: Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; the Āyurvedic account belongs to U30. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Tiruvaḷḷuvar (as a Siddhar)
summary: The Siddha tradition counts Tiruvaḷḷuvar among the Siddhars and ascribes to him works such as the Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam on kāya-siddhi, muppu and vāci; the medicine chapter of the Kuṟaḷ (941–950) is the classical statement of the three humours.
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry and the Kuṟaḷ affiliation dispute.

name: Cuntarāṉantar (Sundarānandar)
summary: Siddhar associated with Madurai: the Siddhar shrine in the Mīṉākṣī temple is linked by tradition with him and with Śiva's sport as the 'all-powerful Siddhar' (ellām valla cittar) who made the stone elephant eat sugarcane.
places: Madurai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The link between the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal episode and this Siddhar is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Rāmatēvar (Irāmatēvar)
summary: Siddhar whose Pūjāviti teaches the worship of the goddess Maṉōṉmaṇi/Vālai at the root; the tradition says he went to Mecca, lived there as 'Yākōpu' and returned, and medical works under that name are ascribed to him.
places: Aḻakar malai (Alagar Kovil) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Mecca/Yākōpu account is the tradition's, recalled at moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kuṭampai (Kutampaic cittar)
summary: Siddhar named from the refrain of his thirty-two couplets, addressed to a girl wearing kuṭampai ear-ornaments; for the realized, he asks, what need of mantra, seals, yoga, rejuvenation or hymns?
places: Māyavaram (Mayiladuthurai) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kamalamuṉi
summary: Siddhar of the popular list, with a samādhi place at Tiruvārūr; no works or teachings are recalled here.
places: Tiruvārūr — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Maccamuṉi (Macchamuni)
summary: Siddhar of the popular list whom the tradition identifies with Matsyendranātha: born as a fish (maccam) that overheard Śiva teaching Pārvatī, and guru of Kōrakkar.
places: Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Identification with tch:matsyendranatha is the tradition's (see brw:natha-tamil-siddha). Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kōrakkar
summary: Siddhar of the popular list whom the tradition identifies with Gorakṣanātha: born from the sacred ash that Maccamuṉi gave a childless woman, who threw it away, until a boy came forth from where it fell. Herbal and alchemical works are ascribed to him; his samādhi is placed at Poyyūr (Vaṭakku Poykainallūr) near Nākappaṭṭiṉam.
places: Vaṭakku Poykainallūr (Poyyūr) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Identification with tch:goraksanatha is the tradition's (see brw:natha-tamil-siddha). Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Aḻukaṇṇi (Aḻukaṇic cittar)
summary: Siddhar poet of forty stanzas in veiled imagery of the root, the six supports and the ninety-six principles, addressed to 'my Kaṇṇammā'; he tells how the guru came, showed his own form and burnt the supports and letters.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Nothing is recalled of his life. The name means 'weeping-eyed'; whether the poet is a man or a woman is not settled here.

name: Kaṭuveḷic cittar
summary: Siddhar poet of the 'Joy-song' (Āṉantak kaḷippu), whose refrain 'do no sin, O mind' and whose image of the mendicant breaking his hard-won pot are among the best-known Siddhar lines.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The name is read as 'the one of the vast (fierce) open space'; no life story is recalled.

name: Akappēyc cittar
summary: Siddhar poet named from his refrain addressing 'akappēy', the demon that is one's own mind.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

name: Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar)
summary: Renouncer-poet: a rich merchant of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam who renounced after his adopted son left him an eyeless needle; his songs on impermanence, the body, women and renunciation are among the most loved in Tamil. Guru of Pattirakiriyār; his samādhi is at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr (Chennai). The tradition treats him as one person with Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai; scholars usually distinguish two or more poets.
places: Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam (Pūmpukār)
Tiruviṭaimarutūr
Ujjain (Ujjaiṉi)
Tiruvoṟṟiyūr — samādhi

scholarly.text: the Siddhar songs c. 14th–17th c.; Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār c. 10th c.

realization_account.text: Childless, Tiruveṇkāṭar received a boy (Śiva's gift, Marutavāṇaṉ) who went trading and returned with cakes of dung; the angry father broke them and found gems. The boy vanished, leaving a box with an eyeless needle and a palm-leaf: 'even an eyeless needle will not come with you on the final road'. He renounced at once; survived his sister's poisoned cake ('one's own deed burns oneself; the baked cake burns the house'); returned to cremate his mother, singing ten songs; at Ujjain was condemned to the stake, which burst into flame, and the king Bhadragiri became his disciple; at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr, playing with boys who covered him with a basket, he vanished and a liṅga was found in his place.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The story is recalled at moderate confidence from the popular hagiography; details vary between tellings.

name: Pattirakiriyār (Bhadragiri)
summary: King of Ujjain turned renouncer and disciple of Paṭṭiṉattār; his 'Lament for true knowledge' asks, in 231 couplets, 'when will the day come' of renunciation, inner yoga and knowledge. The tradition identifies him with Bhartṛhari, king of Ujjain.
places: Ujjain
Tiruviṭaimarutūr — where he attained release (tradition)

realization_account.text: Seeing the stake burn when Paṭṭiṉattār was wrongly condemned, and learning the truth about his court, the king renounced and followed him; living on alms at Tiruviṭaimarutūr, he was chided by his guru for keeping a begging-bowl and a dog ('a householder!'), cast both away, and attained release before his guru.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The identification with Bhartṛhari (tch:bhartrhari) is the tradition's; scholars do not accept it. Story recalled at low–moderate confidence.

name: Tāyumāṉavar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint (early 18th c.) whose songs join Siddhānta and Vedānta in a 'harmony' (camaracam), extol the silent guru and stillness (cummā iruttal), honour the Siddhars, and pray that all beings be happy. Named after Śiva as 'He who became the mother' at the Tiruchirappalli rock temple.
places: Vedāraṇyam (birth, tradition)
Tiruchirappalli (Nāyak court)
Lakṣmīpuram near Rāmanātapuram (samādhi)

realization_account.text: An accountant-minister at the Nāyak court of Tiruchirappalli, he met the silent guru (Mauṉa kuru) of Tirumūlar's line, who told him 'be still' (cummā iru); he later left the court, married at his guru's bidding, and after his wife's death lived as a renouncer until his samādhi near Rāmanātapuram.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Biographical details recalled at moderate–low confidence. Not post-1800, so not flagged recent.

name: Mauṉa kuru (the silent guru of Tāyumāṉavar)
summary: The silent teacher of Tāyumāṉavar at Tiruchirappalli, praised in his songs as coming in Tirumūlar's line (mūlaṉ marapu), who taught by the instruction 'be still'.

name: Pulippāṇi
summary: Disciple of Bogar who, the tradition says, rode a tiger (puli) and carried water for his guru; associated with Palani, where a line of Pulippāṇi priests traced itself to him; medical works bear his name.
places: Palani

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Palani priestly line is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kālāṅki nātar
summary: Siddhar named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage; later tradition makes him the guru of Bogar.
notes: TM 69 (checked locally) names 'Kālāṅki'; the guru-of-Bogar link is the later tradition's.

name: Kañcamalaiyaṉ
summary: Named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage.
notes: Checked in the local TM e-text (69); nothing further recalled.

name: Tēraiyar
summary: Physician-Siddhar, disciple of Agastya, to whom many Siddha medical works are ascribed. The tradition tells that he cured a king by drawing a frog out of his skull with a bowl of water — hence his name ('frog-man').

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Frog story and works recalled at low confidence.

name: Yūkimuṉi
summary: Physician-Siddhar to whom the Yūki vaittiya cintāmaṇi, a standard work on the classification of diseases, is ascribed.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

name: Kākapucuṇṭar (Kākabhuśuṇḍa)
summary: The crow-sage, counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the long-lived crow Bhuśuṇḍa teaches breath-contemplation.
notes: Siddhar-list membership recalled at low confidence.

name: Urōmarisi (Romarishi)
summary: Sage counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; works on medicine and wisdom circulate under his name.
notes: Recalled at low confidence.

name: Pulastiyar
summary: Sage named in Siddha lore as a disciple of Agastya and an authority on medicine.
notes: Recalled at low confidence.

name: Auvaiyār (of the Vināyakar akaval)
summary: The poetess to whom the Vināyakar akaval, a Siddha-revered hymn of the inner yoga, is ascribed; several Tamil poetesses of different centuries bear the name.
